<!-- Copy of cr-poem-og for this section; edit both. -->
冰心《繁星[·]{.interpunct}一》

| 繁星闪烁着——
| 　深蓝的太空，
| 　何曾听得见它们对语？
| 沉默中，
| 　微光里，
| 　　它们深深的互相颂赞了。
:::

:::

# Understanding the poem

:::{.cr-section}

Here are three different translations to try to get at the meaning. @cr-poem-grid-en

The first translation is my own and prioritizes the meaning a Chinese reader would get while sacrificing the experience of an English reader. [@cr-poem-grid-en]{highlight="dav-1,dav-2,dav-3,dav-4,dav-5,dav-6"}

The second is by John Cayley and Grace Boynton and is quite an experience for the English reader but adds meaning not in the original Chinese. [@cr-poem-grid-en]{highlight="cb-1,cb-2,cb-3,cb-4,cb-5,cb-6"}

The third, by Julia C. Lin, retains the simple conciseness of the original but again adds its own meaning. [@cr-poem-grid-en]{highlight="lin-1,lin-2,lin-3,lin-4,lin-5,lin-6"}

And here is a word-by-word translation, to see the meaning as a Chinese reader would. The square brackets \[\] indicate a grammatical term. @cr-poem-gloss

The three translations translate <ruby lang="zh-CN">繁<rt>fán</rt></ruby> three ways: “vast,” “a maze of,” and “infinite.” <ruby lang="zh-CN">繁<rt>fán</rt></ruby> means many, dense, and intricate, and no English word contains all of these meanings. [@cr-poem-grid-en]{highlight="dav-fan,cb-fan,lin-fan"}

Chinese verbs don’t conjugate to carry tense, so tenses, unlike in English, are optional. Tenses are often indicated with additional, optional grammatical markers. <ruby lang="zh-CN">着<rt>zhe</rt></ruby> is one of them and marks an ongoing action. [@cr-poem-gloss]{highlight="g-zhe"}

What is a one-syllable marker in Chinese is either dropped in translation or translated as “continuously,” adding length the original did not have. [@cr-poem-grid-en]{highlight="dav-zhe,cb-zhe,lin-zhe"}

The dash leaves the line open, but only one translation includes it. [@cr-poem-side]{highlight="s-zh-dash,s-dav-dash"}

The entire second line is a noun phrase. [@cr-poem-gloss]{highlight="2"}

The <ruby lang="zh-CN">的<rt>de</rt></ruby> is merely a grammatical character indicating that deep blue (深蓝) is an adjective modifying the noun expanse (太空). [@cr-poem-gloss]{highlight="g-de-2"}

The term <ruby lang="zh-CN">太<rt>tài</rt>空<rt>kōng</rt></ruby> would be understood by a modern Chinese reader as “outer space,” but an early 20th-century reader would have understood it as “expanse,” with a plainer connotation than the English word has. [@cr-poem-gloss]{highlight="g-taikong"}

Chinese does not differentiate between singular and plural nouns, so the line could be translated as “deep blue expanse” or “deep blue expanse**s**.” [@cr-poem-gloss]{highlight="2"}

The parataxis in Chinese is very concise and plain while leaving the relation unstated. [@cr-poem-gloss]{highlight="2"}

The first translation recreates the simplicity but loses some of the connection to the rest of the poem. [@cr-poem-grid-en]{highlight="dav-2"}

The second and third translations set out to capture the feeling of the original by spelling the relation out, but in turn they lose the simplicity of an isolated phrase. [@cr-poem-grid-en]{highlight="cb-2,lin-2"}

Chinese grammar creates an ambiguity that English cannot. The original Chinese line has no subject. [@cr-poem-gloss]{highlight="3"}

This shifts focus from whoever could or could not hear the dialogues to the creators of the dialogues themselves. [@cr-poem-gloss]{highlight="3"}

The closest English can get to this is using the passive voice, as in the first translation, to shift the focus. [@cr-poem-grid-en]{highlight="dav-3"}

In the third line, the term <ruby lang="zh-CN">何<rt>hé</rt>曾<rt>céng</rt></ruby> is a classical rhetorical marker. It contrasts with the modern vernacular of the previous lines. [@cr-poem-gloss]{highlight="g-heceng"}

<ruby lang="zh-CN">听<rt>tīng</rt>得<rt>de</rt>见<rt>jiàn</rt></ruby> doesn’t ask if the dialogues were heard but whether hearing them is possible. [@cr-poem-gloss]{highlight="g-tingdejian"}

<ruby lang="zh-CN">对<rt>duì</rt>语<rt>yǔ</rt></ruby> is an unusual word choice. The more common, conversational term for dialogue or conversation would be <ruby lang="zh-CN">对<rt>duì</rt>话<rt>huà</rt></ruby>. [@cr-poem-gloss]{highlight="g-duiyu"}

<ruby lang="zh-CN">对<rt>duì</rt>语<rt>yǔ</rt></ruby> gives a more literary feel, again making this line feel more formal and older than the rest of the poem. [@cr-poem-gloss]{highlight="g-duiyu"}

Additionally, <ruby lang="zh-CN">对<rt>duì</rt></ruby> means face-to-face or reciprocal, suggesting the dialogues are mutual. [@cr-poem-gloss]{highlight="g-dui"}

<ruby lang="zh-CN">它<rt>tā</rt>们<rt>men</rt></ruby> means “they” in English, but in Chinese it indicates that the “they” are not human. While pronounced the same, Chinese uses <ruby lang="zh-CN">他<rt>tā</rt>们<rt>men</rt></ruby> for human “theys” and <ruby lang="zh-CN">它<rt>tā</rt>们<rt>men</rt></ruby> for animals or inanimate “theys.” [@cr-poem-gloss]{highlight="g-tamen-a"}

None of the translations recreates the contrasting literariness of this line, and the second and third translations add subjects not mentioned in the original. [@cr-poem-grid-en]{highlight="dav-3,cb-3,lin-3"}

Lines four and five have parallel three-character phrases with a noun plus a version of “inside” (中/里). Silence is about sound and glimmer about light, so the poem moves from hearing to seeing. [@cr-poem-gloss]{highlight="g-zhong,g-li"}

It answers the rhetorical question of line three: the stars’ conversations are not heard; instead, they are in silence and light. [@cr-poem-gloss]{highlight="4-5"}

<ruby lang="zh-CN">沉<rt>chén</rt>默<rt>mò</rt></ruby> is an interesting term. <ruby lang="zh-CN">沉<rt>chén</rt></ruby> by itself can mean to sink or submerge (into water), to indulge or to give in to, dark or gloomy, or long and prolonged. [@cr-poem-gloss]{highlight="g-chen"}

<ruby lang="zh-CN">默<rt>mò</rt></ruby> by itself can mean to be silent, or secretly. [@cr-poem-gloss]{highlight="g-mo"}

When combined, the phrase <ruby lang="zh-CN">沉<rt>chén</rt>默<rt>mò</rt></ruby> evokes a feeling of weighted, consuming silence, not just the lack of sound. [@cr-poem-gloss]{highlight="g-chenmo"}

On its own, <ruby lang="zh-CN">微<rt>wēi</rt></ruby> can mean tiny, faint, waning, or obscure. [@cr-poem-gloss]{highlight="g-wei"}

<ruby lang="zh-CN">光<rt>guāng</rt></ruby> means light as a substance, not brightness. [@cr-poem-gloss]{highlight="g-guang"}

When combined, <ruby lang="zh-CN">微<rt>wēi</rt>光<rt>guāng</rt></ruby> means a faint light that feels like it’s barely there. [@cr-poem-gloss]{highlight="g-weiguang"}

<ruby lang="zh-CN">中<rt>zhōng</rt></ruby> and <ruby lang="zh-CN">里<rt>lǐ</rt></ruby> both mean “in” or “within,” but <ruby lang="zh-CN">中<rt>zhōng</rt></ruby> marks an abstract, enclosed space (as silence is a condition you are inside of) while <ruby lang="zh-CN">里<rt>lǐ</rt></ruby> marks a more concrete area (as faint light is a substance you are surrounded by). [@cr-poem-gloss]{highlight="g-zhong,g-li"}

Bing Xin’s choice of <ruby lang="zh-CN">中<rt>zhōng</rt></ruby> for <ruby lang="zh-CN">沉<rt>chén</rt>默<rt>mò</rt></ruby> and <ruby lang="zh-CN">里<rt>lǐ</rt></ruby> for <ruby lang="zh-CN">微<rt>wēi</rt>光<rt>guāng</rt></ruby> is a deliberate asymmetry. [@cr-poem-gloss]{highlight="4-5"}

The English words “in” and “within” only hint at this, and the phonetic contrast is lost. [@cr-poem-grid-en]{highlight="dav-zhong,dav-li,cb-zhong,cb-li,lin-zhong,lin-li"}

Again, Bing Xin uses <ruby lang="zh-CN">它<rt>tā</rt>们<rt>men</rt></ruby>, specifying that the stars are not people. This is in contrast to the personification that immediately follows. [@cr-poem-gloss]{highlight="g-tamen-b"}

For a second time, we see the character <ruby lang="zh-CN">深<rt>shēn</rt></ruby>, meaning deep. In this instance, it is doubled, making it heavier and slower than its first use while describing the depth of the praise. [@cr-poem-gloss]{highlight="g-shen-a,g-shenshen"}

<ruby lang="zh-CN">互<rt>hù</rt>相<rt>xiāng</rt></ruby>, meaning mutually, reminds readers again that the stars’ conversations are reciprocal. [@cr-poem-gloss]{highlight="g-huxiang"}

<ruby lang="zh-CN">颂<rt>sòng</rt>赞<rt>zàn</rt></ruby>, like the word choice in line three, again shifts the poem’s register away from plain and simple. <ruby lang="zh-CN">颂<rt>sòng</rt>赞<rt>zàn</rt></ruby>, meaning to praise or extol, is liturgical. The stars’ praises are devotional worship. [@cr-poem-gloss]{highlight="g-songzan"}

<ruby lang="zh-CN">了<rt>le</rt></ruby> indicates that the worship is complete and the action is no longer ongoing. [@cr-poem-gloss]{highlight="g-le"}

Here we get another answer to the question in line three: the stars are not heard, but they have spoken, and their speech is deep, mutual worship. [@cr-poem-gloss]{highlight="6"}

All the English translations have a lot of active language. [@cr-poem-grid-en]{highlight="dav-act-1,dav-act-6a,dav-act-6b,cb-zhe,cb-act-3,lin-zhe,lin-act-3a,lin-act-3b,lin-act-6a,lin-act-6b"}

The original Chinese, however, has a much more passive feel. Chinese has a tendency to drop the subjects of sentences, meaning that what happens isn’t caused by anything or anyone in particular. @cr-poem-gloss

Only my translation and Lin’s keep Bing Xin’s indents. [@cr-poem-grid]{highlight="ind-zh-2,ind-zh-3,ind-zh-5,ind-zh-6,ind-dav-2,ind-dav-3,ind-dav-5,ind-dav-6,ind-lin-2,ind-lin-3,ind-lin-5,ind-lin-6"}

Even then, they differ: every Chinese character fills the same square, so an indent is exactly one character. English letters vary in width. [@cr-poem-grid]{highlight="ind-zh-2,ind-zh-3,ind-zh-5,ind-zh-6"}

Line length is impossible to match. In Chinese, one character is one syllable, so the lines run five, five, nine, three, three, and ten, on the page and aloud. @cr-poem-grid

:::{#cr-poem-og lang="zh-CN"}

| Vast stars twinkle continuously[—]{#s-dav-dash .dash}
| 　Deep blue space,
| 　Could their words ever be heard?

A Maze of Stars (1) by Bing Xin

| A maze of stars glistens

| In the profound silence,
| in their own faint light,
| this deep acknowledgment of one another.
:::

| Infinite stars sparkle
| 　In the deep blues of sky
| 　Does anyone ever hear them talk?
| In the depths of silence
| 　Within this faint light
| 　　They brightly sing one another's praise.
:::

# Analysis

:::{.cr-section}

A myriad of stars glitter in the sky. No one hears them, but in silence and faint light, they deeply praise each other. @cr-ana-gloss

The stars speak without being heard through silent light. @cr-ana-gloss

The poem starts with light as the stars <ruby lang="zh-CN">闪<rt>shǎn</rt>烁<rt>shuò</rt></ruby> (glitter). Before we even consider if they speak, they are shining without end. [@cr-ana-gloss]{highlight="1"}

The marker <ruby lang="zh-CN">着<rt>zhe</rt></ruby> makes the glittering continuous, so their light, and therefore their speech, never ends. [@cr-ana-gloss]{highlight="a-g-zhe"}

Line three asks if they can be heard. The rhetorical indicator <ruby lang="zh-CN">何<rt>hé</rt>曾<rt>céng</rt></ruby> expects the answer no. [@cr-ana-gloss]{highlight="a-g-heceng"}

The line also has no subject, and therefore no listener. The stars speak to each other and aren’t meant to be heard by us (humans). [@cr-ana-gloss]{highlight="3"}

<ruby lang="zh-CN">它<rt>tā</rt>们<rt>men</rt></ruby> supports this. Bing Xin deliberately chooses a pronoun used for inanimate objects, so human ears are never the audience. [@cr-ana-gloss]{highlight="a-g-tamen-a"}

<ruby lang="zh-CN">对<rt>duì</rt></ruby> in <ruby lang="zh-CN">对<rt>duì</rt>语<rt>yǔ</rt></ruby> means face to face, so we know the stars are talking to each other while we wonder if we can hear them. [@cr-ana-gloss]{highlight="a-g-dui"}

Lines four and five answer the rhetorical question with settings. The stars are in silence and faint light, moving from sound to sight. [@cr-ana-gloss]{highlight="4-5"}

<ruby lang="zh-CN">沉<rt>chén</rt>默<rt>mò</rt></ruby> is a heavy, consuming silence, and <ruby lang="zh-CN">微<rt>wēi</rt>光<rt>guāng</rt></ruby> is a light barely there. The stars speak to each other through almost nothing. [@cr-ana-gloss]{highlight="a-g-chenmo,a-g-weiguang"}

Bing Xin places the stars in silence but surrounded by light. Silence is their condition while light is their medium for their communication. [@cr-ana-gloss]{highlight="a-g-zhong,a-g-li"}

The shape of the poem adds to this. Lines four and five are only three characters each, both short and quiet as the poem itself falls silent. [@cr-ana-gloss]{highlight="4-5"}

Line six confirms their conversations. <ruby lang="zh-CN">互<rt>hù</rt>相<rt>xiāng</rt></ruby> means their conversations are reciprocal with each other and <ruby lang="zh-CN">了<rt>le</rt></ruby> means they’re complete. [@cr-ana-gloss]{highlight="a-g-huxiang,a-g-le"}

<ruby lang="zh-CN">深<rt>shēn</rt>深<rt>shēn</rt></ruby> repeats the <ruby lang="zh-CN">深<rt>shēn</rt></ruby> in “deep blue sky” from line two. The depth of the sky becomes the depth of their praise, and <ruby lang="zh-CN">颂<rt>sòng</rt>赞<rt>zàn</rt></ruby> turns that praise into worship. [@cr-ana-gloss]{highlight="a-g-shen-a,a-g-shenshen,a-g-songzan"}

Line six is the longest line, and ends with a full stop (period) instead of a question mark. The question in line three is answered with this statement: the stars have spoken/ [@cr-ana-gloss]{highlight="3,6"}

Their conversations aren’t heard but are seen by each other through their light. @cr-ana-gloss

Bing Xin suggests that the deepest connections can be seen, not heard. @cr-ana-gloss

:::{#cr-ana-gloss .gloss lang="zh-CN"}

| <ruby>[繁]{#a-g-fan}星<rt>Many stars</rt></ruby><ruby>闪烁<rt>glitter</rt></ruby><ruby>[着]{#a-g-zhe}<rt>[ongoing]</rt></ruby>——
| 　<ruby>[深]{#a-g-shen-a}蓝<rt>deep blue</rt></ruby><ruby>[的]{#a-g-de-2}<rt>[ ]</rt></ruby><ruby>[太空]{#a-g-taikong}<rt>expanse(s)</rt></ruby>，
| 　<ruby>[何曾]{#a-g-heceng}<rt>did ever</rt></ruby><ruby>[听得见]{#a-g-tingdejian}<rt>to be audible</rt></ruby><ruby>[它们]{#a-g-tamen-a}<rt>their</rt></ruby><ruby>[[对]{#a-g-dui}语]{#a-g-duiyu}<rt>dialogue(s)</rt></ruby>？
